evidence: The authorities describe distinct people: n80020492/Q962080 is Peter Brown (born 1935), author of Augustine of Hippo (1967) and the late-antiquity books; n50039584 is Peter Hume Brown (1849–1918), author of George Buchanan (1890) and History of Scotland. The later Scottish editions are reprints, not evidence of one career.

a is Connecticut urban historian Peter C. Baldwin, author of Domesticating the Street. b mainly represents UCLA welfare-state historian Peter Baldwin, but its How Night Air Became Good Air (2003) is explicitly credited by the publisher to Peter C. Baldwin at Connecticut. n99025329/Q110669337 and n88275684/Q7172657 represent distinct people; b mixes their works.

n94054333/Q6327586 identifies Robert David (KC) Johnson at Brooklyn College, whose Senate dissertation, Peace Progressives and Congress and the Cold War form a US diplomatic-history career. nb99182873/Q99388792 identifies Oxford military historian Rob Johnson, author of The Afghan Way of War and British Imperialism. The authority records represent distinct people, not duplicates.

a mixes the geographer who wrote The Limits to Capital with David Allen Harvey’s Lahontan article (2010), as well as a 1912 medical paper. The checked authorities are distinct: n50028377/Q343055 is the geographer born 1935; no99026022 is David Allen Harvey, born 1971, whose Alsace dissertation and French-cultural-history books appear under b.

n50056863/Q7351081 represents Robert William Davies (1925–2021), the Soviet economic historian whose works include The Soviet Collective Farm and The Years of Hunger. n77007222/Q7306966 represents Robert Rees Davies (1938–2005), the medievalist who wrote Lordship and Society in the March of Wales and The Revolt of Owain Glyn Dŵr. These are distinct authority identities and careers.

b combines the Latin American literature/cinema scholar’s Sur and Magical Reels with The Light of Printing (2001), explicitly authored by John N. King, whose Reformation books are under a. Checked n81143090/Q87185921 identifies the Reformation scholar (1945–2020); n85377106/Q112355950 identifies Warwick’s Latin Americanist (born 1950). The authorities are distinct; b is contaminated.

a’s sole item concerns nineteenth-century kidnapping and the Joseph Watson papers; the university bibliographic record credits its modern editor/author as Eric Ledell Smith, so the Henderson attribution is unreliable. b is the classicist J. G. W. Henderson (Q1426806), author of Fighting for Rome and Writing Down Rome. This citation supplies no connection to that classical-scholarship career.

The checked identities are distinct: n2005019160/Q92595039 is Edward Jay Watts (born 1975), the UCSD ancient historian whose 2002 dissertation became City and School. no93001940 identifies Edward Watts (born 1964), Michigan State English professor; its LC notes explicitly list Writing and Postcolonialism, An American Colony and In This Remote Country, the works under b.

a’s 2006 and 2009 architecture articles belong to Oxford historian William Whyte, author of b’s Oxford Jackson; the publisher identifies his Oxford affiliation. But a also includes a Bennett Law article published in 1927, decades before this historian’s 1975 birth (Q55781336). The corpus key therefore combines different authors.

Goldsmiths lists both b’s Jamaican Volunteers (2004) and a’s West Indians at War (2008) under Richard W. P. Smith. But a also contains medieval demographic/property scholarship and an airliner-performance article credited to Richard K. Smith. Only the Caribbean military-history component matches b; merging the whole key would combine multiple authors.

The main authority identities are different: n2007021376 is John Craig Hammond (born 1974), author of the 2004 dissertation and 2007 slavery book; n50020022/Q6244194 is British labour historian John Lawrence Hammond (1872–1949). b additionally contains Revival Religion and Antislavery Politics (1974), by the modern sociologist John L. Hammond. Thus b itself mixes people and cannot be merged with a.

b is the documented Labour politician James Ramsay MacDonald (1866–1937), whose political books form a coherent career. a has no works and only the name-based corpus anchor macdonald|james. Searching confirms b’s full name but supplies no work, date or institutional anchor identifying a; the initial and compatible name cannot establish identity.

The publisher confirms David R. Murray as author of Odious Commerce; catalogues also credit Colonial Justice to David Murray/David Robert Murray. However, a has no works and only the name-based corpus anchor murray|david. No supplied or located fact ties that bare corpus identity to this author, so the name variant alone cannot justify a merge.

a combines colonial-Peru articles with British-diplomacy books such as Curzon and British Imperialism. Its n98040947/Q95240460 identifies John Fisher, born 1968; b’s n80144300/Q116483742 identifies John Robert Fisher, born 1943, the Peru specialist. These are distinct authority identities. The 1975 Peru article cannot belong to the seven-year-old future diplomacy historian, so a mixes careers.

Michael Crawford’s Academia Europaea bibliography lists a’s exact 1974 article, coauthored with Mark Hassall and Joyce Reynolds, alongside b’s Roman Republican Coinage (1974), Roman Republican Coin Hoards (1969), and other Roman-history works. This directly places the sole M. H. Crawford citation within Michael Hewson Crawford’s documented publication record.
